options.a: Adductor longus
options.b: Gluteus maximus
options.c: Rectus femoris
options.d: Gluteus medius

distractorExplanations.a: Adductor longus adducts the hip and assists flexion; the gluteus maximus is the prime mover for hip extension.
distractorExplanations.c: Rectus femoris crosses the hip anteriorly and flexes it (and extends the knee); it opposes hip extension.
distractorExplanations.d: Gluteus medius is the primary hip abductor and frontal-plane stabilizer, not the main hip extensor.

options.a: Slow-twitch, fatigue-resistant fibers
options.b: Fast-twitch fibers with high force output
options.c: Fast-twitch fibers with moderate fatigue resistance
options.d: Slow-twitch fibers with low capillary density

distractorExplanations.b: High force, fast-twitch fibers that fatigue quickly are Type IIx, the opposite end from Type I.
distractorExplanations.c: Fast-twitch fibers with moderate fatigue resistance describe Type IIa, an intermediate fiber type.
distractorExplanations.d: Type I fibers have high capillary and mitochondrial density, which is what makes them fatigue-resistant.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-basics-anatomy-.explanation: Type I fibers are slow-twitch, oxidative and fatigue-resistant, used heavily in endurance and postural work; Type II are faster and more fatigable.

options.a: Myofibril
options.b: Sarcomere
options.c: Motor unit
options.d: Fascicle

distractorExplanations.a: A myofibril is a chain of many sarcomeres in series; the sarcomere is the smallest contractile unit.
distractorExplanations.c: A motor unit is one motor neuron plus the fibers it innervates, a neural control unit, not a structure within a fiber.
distractorExplanations.d: A fascicle is a bundle of whole muscle fibers, a much larger level of organization than the sarcomere.

options.a: A strength exercise followed by a stabilization exercise for the same pattern
options.b: Two heavy strength exercises for the same muscle group
options.c: A heavy strength exercise with a lighter, high-velocity power exercise
options.d: Single heavy lifts at 85–100% 1RM with full rest and no power work

distractorExplanations.a: Pairing strength with a stabilization exercise is the Phase 2 (Strength Endurance) superset, not Phase 5 Power.
distractorExplanations.b: Back-to-back strength exercises for one muscle group fit hypertrophy work in Phase 3, not power training.
distractorExplanations.d: Heavy lifts at 85–100% with no power exercise describe Phase 4 Maximal Strength.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-basics-anatomy-.explanation: Power phases use complex/contrast pairing of a heavy strength exercise with a lighter, high-velocity power exercise for the same movement pattern, after foundations are built.

options.a: Provide deep local stabilization
options.b: Act as prime mover for trunk flexion
options.c: Rotate the trunk as a global mover
options.d: Extend the spine under heavy load

distractorExplanations.b: Trunk flexion as a prime mover is the rectus abdominis, a global muscle, not the deep transverse abdominis.
distractorExplanations.c: Trunk rotation is driven by the obliques in the global system; the TrA is a local stabilizer.
distractorExplanations.d: Spinal extension under load is the erector spinae's job; the TrA braces rather than extends the spine.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-basics-anatomy-.explanation: TrA is a local stabilizer that increases intra-abdominal pressure and braces the lumbar spine for segmental control; global movers create larger trunk motions.

options.a: It is fully shortened with maximal filament overlap
options.b: It is stretched well past resting length
options.c: Actin and myosin have an optimal overlap
options.d: Its antagonist is shortened and fully active

distractorExplanations.a: Excess overlap at full shortening crowds the filaments and reduces cross-bridges; more overlap is not more force.
distractorExplanations.b: Stretching far past resting length leaves too little actin–myosin overlap, so fewer cross-bridges form.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses length–tension with reciprocal inhibition; a tight antagonist actually alters length and reduces force.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-basics-anatomy-.explanation: Force peaks near optimal sarcomere length (near resting length), where actin and myosin overlap optimally; too short or too long reduces cross-bridge capacity.

options.a: Local stabilization system muscles
options.b: Global muscular subsystems
options.c: The central nervous system's motor control
options.d: Passive ligamentous stabilizing system

distractorExplanations.a: The local system (TrA, multifidus, pelvic floor) gives segmental stability; DLS belongs to the global subsystems.
distractorExplanations.c: The CNS directs movement, but DLS is a muscular subsystem that transfers force through the kinetic chain.
distractorExplanations.d: Ligaments are passive restraints; the DLS is a chain of muscles (peroneals, tibialis anterior, biceps femoris, erector spinae).

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-basics-anatomy-.explanation: Local and global muscular subsystems (including DLS, POS, AOS, LS) describe force transfer and stabilization roles; the DLS is one of the global subsystems that transfer force across the kinetic chain.

options.a: Anterior and posterior tibialis with the medial gastrocnemius
options.b: Soleus / lateral gastrocnemius and/or biceps femoris (short head)
options.c: Hip flexor complex, latissimus dorsi, and erector spinae
options.d: Adductor complex, TFL, and vastus lateralis

distractorExplanations.a: Tibialis and medial gastrocnemius are typically underactive (not overactive) in foot-turn-out and flattening patterns.
distractorExplanations.c: Overactive hip flexors, lats, and erector spinae describe the low-back-arches compensation, not feet turning out.
distractorExplanations.d: Overactive adductors, TFL, and vastus lateralis are the knee valgus (knees move in) pattern.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-assessment-002.explanation: Foot/ankle compensation patterns often involve lateral calf and biceps femoris overactivity, with underactive medial gastrocnemius, medial hamstrings, gracilis, sartorius, and popliteus.

options.a: Static postural assessment
options.b: Shark skill test
options.c: 1RM back squat test
options.d: Overhead squat assessment

distractorExplanations.a: A static postural assessment observes alignment at rest, not dynamic movement of the kinetic chain.
distractorExplanations.b: The shark skill test measures lower-extremity agility and neuromuscular control in hops, not loaded postural compensation.
distractorExplanations.c: A 1RM test measures maximal strength; it is not a structured observation of movement compensations.

options.a: Gluteus medius / maximus
options.b: Adductor complex and TFL
options.c: Hip flexors and erector spinae
options.d: Soleus and lateral gastrocnemius

distractorExplanations.b: The adductors and TFL are typically overactive in knee valgus; they pull the knee inward.
distractorExplanations.c: Overactive hip flexors and erector spinae go with the low back arching compensation, not knee valgus.
distractorExplanations.d: Overactive soleus and lateral gastrocnemius are linked to feet turning out, and they are overactive, not underactive.

options.a: Estimate VO2max from a submaximal field test
options.b: Screen for health risks before exercise
options.c: Document the client's training goals and preferences
options.d: Serve as the signed informed consent waiver

distractorExplanations.a: VO2max estimates come from field tests like Rockport or the step test; the PAR-Q+ is a health questionnaire.
distractorExplanations.c: Goals and preferences are gathered in a general and lifestyle intake, not by the PAR-Q+ readiness screen.
distractorExplanations.d: Informed consent is a separate legal document; the PAR-Q+ screens risk and does not replace it.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-assessment-006.explanation: Preparticipation screening tools identify red flags and whether medical clearance or modified programming is needed; they do not replace clinical diagnosis or all legal forms.

options.a: Suprailiac skinfold
options.b: Midaxillary line
options.c: Waist
options.d: Subscapular point

distractorExplanations.a: Suprailiac is a skinfold caliper site, not a circumference (tape) measurement site.
distractorExplanations.b: The midaxillary line is a skinfold site used in caliper protocols, not a tape circumference site.
distractorExplanations.d: The subscapular site is pinched in skinfold protocols; circumference formulas use tape sites such as the waist.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-assessment-007.explanation: Waist, hip, neck, and limb sites appear in various circumference protocols; choose the protocol's sites. Skinfold caliper sites are a different method.

options.a: Middle and lower trapezius
options.b: Pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi
options.c: Rhomboids and serratus anterior
options.d: Upper trapezius / levator scapulae

distractorExplanations.a: Mid and lower trapezius are typically underactive when the shoulders elevate, not overactive.
distractorExplanations.b: Overactive pecs and lats are linked to arms falling forward or rounded shoulders, not shoulder elevation.
distractorExplanations.c: Rhomboids and serratus are scapular stabilizers usually targeted for activation, not the overactive elevators.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-assessment-008.explanation: Scapular elevation compensations often involve upper trap/levator overactivity, with underactive mid/lower trapezius.

options.a: Uncontrolled hypertension may require medical clearance
options.b: Resting BP sets the client's target heart rate zones
options.c: Low resting BP means the client can skip warm-ups
options.d: BP readings establish the client's VO2max estimate

distractorExplanations.b: Heart rate zones come from max HR or HR reserve formulas, not from blood pressure readings.
distractorExplanations.c: A low reading does not remove the need for a warm-up; BP is screened for risk, not to trim session parts.
distractorExplanations.d: VO2max is estimated from cardio tests using heart rate or time; blood pressure is not an input.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-assessment-009.explanation: Uncontrolled hypertension is a risk factor that may require medical clearance and intensity modification; trainers refer as indicated.

options.a: Anaerobic power from a timed 400-meter sprint
options.b: Cardiorespiratory fitness from a timed 1-mile walk
options.c: Agility from timed cone changes of direction
options.d: Cardiorespiratory fitness from a 3-minute step test

distractorExplanations.a: The Rockport test is a submaximal walk; a 400 m sprint measures anaerobic capacity, a different test.
distractorExplanations.c: Timed cone drills such as the LEF or pro shuttle test agility; Rockport estimates aerobic fitness.
distractorExplanations.d: The 3-minute step test is the YMCA step protocol; Rockport uses a timed 1-mile walk and heart rate.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-assessment-010.explanation: Field walk tests estimate aerobic fitness without a full lab VO2 protocol; Rockport gives a VO2-related estimate from a timed 1-mile walk and heart rate.

options.a: Tight upper trapezius and pectorals with weak deep neck flexors and lower trapezius
options.b: Tight gluteus maximus and abdominals with weak hip flexors and erector spinae
options.c: Tight hip flexors and erector spinae with weak gluteus maximus and abdominals
options.d: Tight adductors and TFL with weak gluteus medius and vastus medialis oblique

distractorExplanations.a: That pattern is upper crossed syndrome, the shoulder and neck counterpart to lower crossed syndrome.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the pairs: in lower crossed syndrome the hip flexors and erectors are tight and the glutes and abdominals weak.
distractorExplanations.d: Tight adductors/TFL with weak glute medius and VMO is the pronation distortion or knee valgus pattern.

options.a: Reduce the range of motion and finish the test
options.b: Switch to the opposite limb and continue
options.c: Ice the joint and retest after a short rest
options.d: Stop the painful movement and refer out

distractorExplanations.a: Sharp pain is a stop signal; shrinking the range and continuing still loads a possibly injured joint.
distractorExplanations.b: Moving to the other side ignores a warning sign that needs referral before further testing.
distractorExplanations.c: Icing and retesting treats and re-provokes a possible injury; the trainer stops and refers instead.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-assessment-012.explanation: Sharp pain is a stop-and-refer cue: stop the painful movement and refer out or seek medical clearance as appropriate; trainers do not diagnose injuries.

options.a: Upper-body agility and stabilization
options.b: Lower-body reactive agility and quickness
options.c: Upper-body muscular endurance to failure
options.d: Core endurance in a timed plank hold

distractorExplanations.b: Lower-body agility is tested with the shark skill test; Davies is an upper-extremity test in a push-up position.
distractorExplanations.c: Push-ups to failure test muscular endurance; Davies counts alternating hand touches over 15 seconds.
distractorExplanations.d: A static plank hold measures core endurance; Davies adds reactive hand movement for shoulder stability and agility.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-assessment-013.explanation: Davies test challenges upper-body agility and shoulder stabilization with reactive hand touches in a plank position.

options.a: Arms falling forward and low back arching
options.b: Knee valgus / hip drop / trunk lean
options.c: Shoulder elevation and head jutting forward
options.d: Feet flattening on both sides at once

distractorExplanations.a: Arms falling forward and low back arching are overhead squat findings, not the single-leg squat checkpoints.
distractorExplanations.c: Shoulder elevation and forward head are watched in pushing and pulling assessments, not the single-leg squat.
distractorExplanations.d: A single-leg squat loads one limb, so a bilateral foot finding cannot appear; it belongs to the overhead squat.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-assessment-014.explanation: SLS reveals frontal-plane control deficits such as knee valgus, hip drop, and trunk lean, depending on observation.

options.a: A direct measure of body fat percentage from skinfolds
options.b: A waist-to-hip ratio that predicts visceral fat risk
options.c: A height–weight ratio that estimates weight category risk
options.d: A height–weight ratio that separates fat mass from muscle

distractorExplanations.a: Body fat percentage from skinfolds is a separate method; BMI uses only height and weight.
distractorExplanations.b: Waist-to-hip ratio is a different circumference index; BMI is weight (kg) divided by height (m) squared.
distractorExplanations.d: BMI cannot distinguish fat from muscle, which is why muscular athletes are often misclassified.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-assessment-015.explanation: BMI screens weight status from height and weight but does not measure body fat directly; athletes and older adults may be misclassified versus true composition.

options.a: 12–20 reps, 1–3 sets, slow tempos, shorter rest, lower intensity
options.b: 1–5 reps, 4–6 sets, explosive tempo, 3–5 min rest, 85–100% 1RM
options.c: 6–12 reps, 3–5 sets, moderate tempo, 0–60 s rest, 75–85% 1RM
options.d: 8–12 reps, 2–4 sets, moderate tempo, 0–60 s rest, 70–80% 1RM

distractorExplanations.b: Heavy 1–5 rep sets with long rest are Phase 4 Maximal Strength, not Phase 1 Stabilization Endurance.
distractorExplanations.c: 6–12 reps at 75–85% with 3–5 sets are the Phase 3 Muscular Development (hypertrophy) variables.
distractorExplanations.d: 8–12 reps at 70–80% in supersets are Phase 2 Strength Endurance variables, used after stabilization.

options.a: Ball crunches / back extensions / reverse crunches
options.b: Floor bridges / dead bugs / bird dogs
options.c: Cable rotations / cable lifts and chops
options.d: Medicine ball rotation chest passes / soccer throws

distractorExplanations.a: Ball crunches and back extensions are core-strength level exercises with spinal motion, after stabilization.
distractorExplanations.c: Cable rotations and lift-and-chop patterns are core-strength exercises, too advanced for the stabilization start.
distractorExplanations.d: Medicine ball throws are core-power exercises for Phase 5, the last level of core progression.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-program-design-.explanation: Start with controlled anti-extension/anti-rotation stability (floor bridges, dead bugs, bird dogs) before loaded spinal flexion machines or aggressive trunk work.

options.a: Strength, accuracy, and quality of movement
options.b: Stabilization, agility, and quickness
options.c: Speed, agility, and quickness
options.d: Speed, aerobic capacity, and quickness

distractorExplanations.a: Misreads the acronym; SAQ stands for speed, agility, and quickness, not strength or accuracy.
distractorExplanations.b: Swaps speed for stabilization; stabilization is a separate OPT phase, and SAQ's S is speed.
distractorExplanations.d: Swaps agility for aerobic capacity; SAQ's A is agility, the ability to change direction.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-program-design-.explanation: SAQ drills improve speed, agility, and quickness (acceleration, change of direction, and reaction) alongside other programming.

options.a: Inhibit/lengthen mid/lower trapezius and rhomboids; activate the latissimus dorsi
options.b: Inhibit/lengthen hip flexors and latissimus dorsi; activate gluteus maximus and core
options.c: Inhibit/lengthen upper trapezius and levator scapulae; activate deep neck flexors
options.d: Inhibit/lengthen latissimus dorsi and pectorals; activate mid/lower trapezius

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the plan: the lats are overactive and need lengthening, while mid/lower traps and rhomboids need activation.
distractorExplanations.b: Hip flexor lengthening with glute and core activation is the low-back-arches correction, not arms falling forward.
distractorExplanations.c: Upper trap/levator lengthening with deep neck flexor work targets shoulder elevation and forward head.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-program-design-.explanation: Arms-fall-forward often involves tight lats/pecs and weak scapular retractors/depressors: inhibit/lengthen latissimus dorsi and pectorals, then activate/integrate mid/lower trapezius and rhomboids as indicated.

options.a: Approximately 6–12 reps at moderate-to-challenging loads
options.b: Approximately 8–10 reps at light loads moved explosively
options.c: Approximately 12–20 reps at light-to-moderate loads
options.d: Approximately 20–30 reps with minimal rest for toning

distractorExplanations.b: 8–10 explosive reps at light loads (30–45% 1RM) are the power exercise in Phase 5, not hypertrophy work.
distractorExplanations.c: 12–20 reps at lighter loads are the Phase 1 Stabilization Endurance range, not muscular development.
distractorExplanations.d: Very high reps with light loads build local endurance; hypertrophy needs enough tension in the 6–12 range.

options.a: Lengthen muscles with long static holds to prevent strains during heavy lifting
options.b: Increase tissue temperature, nervous system readiness, and movement-specific ROM
options.c: Pre-fatigue the target muscles so the working sets recruit more fibers
options.d: Lower heart rate and promote recovery from the previous training session

distractorExplanations.a: Long static holds before lifting can briefly reduce force output; a dynamic warm-up uses active movement.
distractorExplanations.c: Pre-exhaustion is a training technique; a warm-up should prepare tissues without creating fatigue.
distractorExplanations.d: Bringing heart rate down and aiding recovery is the purpose of a cool-down, not a pre-session warm-up.

options.a: Complete a 1RM squat of at least 1.5 times body weight
options.b: Perform several high-volume sets of jumps without noticeable fatigue
options.c: Demonstrate adequate strength, landing mechanics, and joint stability
options.d: Hold a single-leg balance for 30 seconds with eyes closed

distractorExplanations.a: The 1.5x body-weight squat is an old fixed rule for advanced depth jumps, not the general entry criterion.
distractorExplanations.b: Jump volume tolerance is built through progression; readiness depends on landing control and stability first.
distractorExplanations.d: Balance holds are part of the foundation but do not show the landing mechanics and strength plyometrics require.

options.a: About 0–60 seconds
options.b: About 60–90 seconds
options.c: About 90–120 seconds
options.d: About 3–5 minutes

distractorExplanations.a: 0–60 seconds of rest fits stabilization and strength endurance work, not heavy maximal strength sets.
distractorExplanations.b: 60–90 seconds is too short for ATP–PC restoration between near-maximal sets; it suits hypertrophy-style work.
distractorExplanations.c: Under 2 minutes does not fully restore ATP–PC stores for 85–100% 1RM sets; maximal strength needs 3–5 minutes.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-program-design-.explanation: High-load strength work needs longer rest than endurance circuits: about 3–5 minutes for neural and ATP–PC restoration between maximal sets.

options.a: Bodyweight squat → goblet squat → barbell variations
options.b: Barbell back squat → goblet squat → bodyweight squat
options.c: Single-leg BOSU squat → bodyweight squat → barbell squat
options.d: Leg press to failure → Smith machine squat → barbell squat

distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the progression; load and complexity should increase only after bodyweight pattern competency.
distractorExplanations.c: Starting on an unstable single-leg surface is far too advanced before a stable bilateral pattern is learned.
distractorExplanations.d: Machine work to failure does not teach the free squat pattern; progression starts with bodyweight technique.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-program-design-.explanation: Progress complexity and load after pattern competency: bodyweight or assisted box squat, then goblet squat, then barbell variations as technique allows.

options.a: Load should rise by 10% every week for steady gains
options.b: Training stress must gradually increase over time
options.c: Volume should stay fixed while only load increases
options.d: Each session should reach muscular failure to force adaptation

distractorExplanations.a: A fixed weekly percentage ignores recovery and plateaus; overload can come from load, volume, density, or complexity.
distractorExplanations.c: Load is one lever; volume, density, and exercise complexity are also valid ways to progress overload.
distractorExplanations.d: Failure is not required for overload; gradual increases within recovery capacity drive adaptation.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-program-design-.explanation: Adaptation requires progressive challenge: training stress must gradually increase via load, volume, density, or complexity over time, within recovery capacity and not by chasing pain.

options.a: Burns more calories per session than steady-state cardio
options.b: Reduces fat locally from the muscles being trained
options.c: Helps preserve lean mass in a calorie deficit
options.d: Converts stored fat directly into new muscle tissue

distractorExplanations.a: Calories burned per session are often similar or lower than cardio; the key benefit is preserving lean mass.
distractorExplanations.b: Spot reduction is a myth; fat is lost systemically, not from the area being exercised.
distractorExplanations.d: Fat and muscle are different tissues; fat cannot be converted into muscle.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-program-design-.explanation: Resistance training protects muscle during weight loss and supports metabolic rate in a calorie deficit; nutrition and cardio still matter.

options.a: Inhale deeply during the concentric push
options.b: Hold the breath for the entire set
options.c: Exhale fully before starting the lift
options.d: Brace and exhale through the sticking point

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the usual pattern; air is typically drawn in on the eccentric and exhaled through the concentric effort.
distractorExplanations.b: Prolonged breath-holding spikes blood pressure; Valsalva is brief and only for suitable advanced lifters.
distractorExplanations.c: Emptying the lungs before the lift removes the brace that supports the spine under load.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-program-design-.explanation: Bracing with controlled breathing manages intra-abdominal pressure: brace and exhale through the sticking point, avoiding prolonged breath-holding if contraindicated.

options.a: Combining flexibility, core, balance, SAQ, plyometric, and resistance training
options.b: Combining resistance training and cardio in the same session
options.c: Progressing every client through all five OPT phases in strict order
options.d: Blending machine, free-weight, and cable resistance exercises into one circuit

distractorExplanations.b: Pairing lifting and cardio is concurrent training; NASM integrated training spans all the OPT components.
distractorExplanations.c: Integrated training combines components; clients move between phases based on goals rather than in a fixed sequence.
distractorExplanations.d: Mixing equipment covers only the resistance component; integration also includes flexibility, core, balance, SAQ, and plyometrics.

options.a: A planned increase in volume before a testing week
options.b: A planned reduction in volume and/or intensity
options.c: A full week off from all training to reset
options.d: A reduction in calories to cut body weight

distractorExplanations.a: A planned volume spike is functional overreaching; a deload reduces training load.
distractorExplanations.c: A deload keeps some training stimulus; complete rest is a separate recovery choice.
distractorExplanations.d: Calorie reduction is a diet phase; a deload changes training volume and intensity.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-program-design-.explanation: Deloads are a planned reduction in volume and/or intensity that manage fatigue for recovery and adaptation while keeping some training stimulus.

options.a: Provide general healthy eating guidelines and refer to an RD
options.b: Write a calorie-specific meal plan for a client's diabetes
options.c: Design a low-sodium diet to treat a client's hypertension
options.d: Recommend a supplement stack to correct a client's anemia

distractorExplanations.b: A disease-specific meal plan is medical nutrition therapy, which requires a registered dietitian.
distractorExplanations.c: Treating hypertension with a prescribed diet is medical nutrition therapy, outside CPT scope.
distractorExplanations.d: Correcting anemia is medical treatment that needs diagnosis and care from a licensed clinician.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-nutrition-biz-0.explanation: CPTs educate with general healthy eating guidelines and refer to an RD for medical nutrition therapy; disease-specific MNT and diagnosis are for licensed clinicians.

options.a: About 0.5–0.7 g/kg/day for most lifters
options.b: About 0.8 g/kg/day, the same as the RDA
options.c: About 1.2–2.2 g/kg/day depending on goals
options.d: About 3.5–4.5 g/kg/day for muscle gain

distractorExplanations.a: 0.5–0.7 g/kg/day is below even the sedentary RDA and too low to support training recovery.
distractorExplanations.b: 0.8 g/kg/day is the RDA for sedentary adults; exercising adults usually need more.
distractorExplanations.d: Intakes above about 2.2 g/kg/day add little benefit for most people and displace other nutrients.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-nutrition-biz-0.explanation: Active individuals usually need about 1.2–2.2 g/kg/day depending on goals and total energy intake, more than sedentary RDAs; extreme values are unnecessary or unrealistic.

options.a: Broad outcome goals reviewed once a year
options.b: Motivation from before-and-after photos alone
options.c: Long-term weight-loss targets without any weekly action steps
options.d: Specific, measurable action plans and self-monitoring

distractorExplanations.a: Distant, broad goals lack the specific steps and frequent feedback that turn intentions into behavior.
distractorExplanations.b: Photos may inspire, but without action plans and self-monitoring they rarely change daily behavior.
distractorExplanations.c: Outcome targets without process steps leave clients unsure what to do each week.

options.a: Disclosure is required by law or the client provides consent
options.b: Another trainer at your gym asks for the client's health history
options.c: The client's employer requests their attendance records
options.d: The information helps you market your training results

distractorExplanations.b: Colleagues have no right to client health details without consent, even within the same facility.
distractorExplanations.c: An employer request is not a legal requirement or client consent, so records stay confidential.
distractorExplanations.d: Marketing benefit does not justify disclosure; client details and results need written consent.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-nutrition-biz-0.explanation: Privacy is an ethical/legal duty; limited exceptions exist when disclosure is required by law or duty-to-warn situations, or when the client provides appropriate consent.

options.a: Recommend specific doses since supplements are FDA-approved before sale
options.b: Discuss general evidence cautiously and refer to qualified professionals
options.c: Sell supplements with disease-treatment claims if a study supports them
options.d: Prescribe a creatine dose to every client to improve performance results

distractorExplanations.a: The FDA does not approve dietary supplements before sale, and dosing advice is outside CPT scope.
distractorExplanations.c: Disease-treatment claims are prohibited for supplements, and making them is outside a trainer's scope.
distractorExplanations.d: Prescribing supplements is clinical practice; a CPT shares general evidence and refers.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-nutrition-biz-0.explanation: Supplement advice has legal/ethical limits: discuss general evidence cautiously, refer clients to qualified professionals, and do not prescribe like a clinician; disease claims and invasive procedures are out of scope.

options.a: Specific, Motivating, Achievable, Rewarding, Timed
options.b: Simple, Meaningful, Adaptable, Realistic/Rewarding, Time-limited
options.c: Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Realistic/Relevant, Time-bound
options.d: Specific, Manageable, Accurate, Ranked, Trackable

distractorExplanations.a: Motivating and Rewarding are not SMART letters; M is Measurable and R is Realistic or Relevant.
distractorExplanations.b: S stands for Specific, not Simple; M is Measurable, not Meaningful; and A is Attainable rather than Adaptable.
distractorExplanations.d: Mixes up the letters: M is Measurable, A Attainable, R Realistic/Relevant, and T Time-bound.

options.a: Results guarantees in contracts to build client confidence
options.b: Verbal-only agreements to keep the client relationship informal and flexible
options.c: Testimonials edited to show the most dramatic outcomes
options.d: Clear contracts, transparent pricing, and accurate marketing claims

distractorExplanations.a: Guaranteeing results is a misleading claim that creates liability; outcomes depend on many factors.
distractorExplanations.b: Verbal-only agreements leave terms, cancellations, and scope undocumented, which invites disputes.
distractorExplanations.c: Editing testimonials to exaggerate results is deceptive marketing, not accurate claims.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-nutrition-biz-0.explanation: Professional practice requires honesty, consent, and legal compliance: clear contracts, transparent pricing, documented scope of practice, and accurate marketing claims.

options.a: Collaborative, client-centered exploration of ambivalence
options.b: Directive advice that tells clients exactly what to change
options.c: Rewards and incentives that build extrinsic motivation
options.d: Confronting resistance with evidence until the client agrees

distractorExplanations.b: Telling clients what to change is the directing style that MI replaces with collaboration.
distractorExplanations.c: MI evokes the client's own intrinsic reasons for change rather than relying on external rewards.
distractorExplanations.d: Arguing against resistance increases it; MI rolls with resistance and explores ambivalence.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-nutrition-biz-0.explanation: MI uses empathy, evocative questions, and partnership to explore ambivalence and intrinsic motivation rather than confrontation alone.

options.a: Raising plasma volume and slowing heart rate at a given pace
options.b: Reducing plasma volume and impairing thermoregulation
options.c: Increasing sweat rate and improving heat dissipation
options.d: Lowering core temperature and blood viscosity

distractorExplanations.a: Dehydration lowers plasma volume, which raises heart rate at a given workload (cardiovascular drift).
distractorExplanations.c: Fluid loss reduces sweat rate and skin blood flow, so heat dissipation gets worse, not better.
distractorExplanations.d: Dehydration raises core temperature and blood viscosity rather than lowering them.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-nutrition-biz-0.explanation: Fluid deficits reduce plasma volume, increase cardiovascular strain (higher heart rate for a given workload), impair thermoregulation, and raise heat illness risk.

options.a: Did you manage to complete all three of your planned workouts this week?
options.b: Was the cardio harder than last week's session?
options.c: What barriers got in the way of your workouts this week?
options.d: How many workouts did you finish this week?

distractorExplanations.a: A did-you question invites a yes/no reply, making it closed-ended despite the longer wording.
distractorExplanations.b: This invites a yes/no comparison, so it is closed rather than open-ended.
distractorExplanations.d: A how-many question asks for a single number, a closed question that limits reflection.

options.a: Write a low-carb meal plan to bring their blood sugar down
options.b: Adjust their meal timing around their medication doses
options.c: Provide a diabetic exchange-list diet from a trainer handout
options.d: Refer to a registered dietitian / physician

distractorExplanations.a: A diet designed to treat blood sugar is medical nutrition therapy, outside CPT scope.
distractorExplanations.b: Coordinating food with diabetes medication is clinical management for a physician or RD.
distractorExplanations.c: Exchange-list diets are disease-specific MNT tools that require a registered dietitian.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-nutrition-biz-0.explanation: Diabetes MNT and medication management require licensed clinicians: refer to a registered dietitian or physician for medical nutrition therapy and stay within general guidelines.

options.a: Prioritize sleep, progressive programming, and adequate nutrition/hydration
options.b: Prioritize daily foam rolling, cold plunges, and supplements over sleep
options.c: Train hard every day and use caffeine to offset short sleep
options.d: Rely on complete rest weeks instead of planned progressive loading

distractorExplanations.b: Modalities like rolling and cold plunges are adjuncts; they cannot replace sleep as the recovery foundation.
distractorExplanations.c: Caffeine masks fatigue but does not restore recovery; short sleep impairs adaptation and raises injury risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Recovery is built into progressive programming; random full-rest weeks do not replace planned loading.

options.a: Relies on the gym's general insurance instead of screening
options.b: Screens clients, documents sessions, and stays in scope
options.c: Has clients sign a waiver and skips health screening
options.d: Gives advice outside scope only when a client insists

distractorExplanations.a: Insurance pays claims but does not reduce risk; screening and documentation prevent incidents.
distractorExplanations.c: A waiver does not replace screening; skipping it misses red flags and weakens a negligence defense.
distractorExplanations.d: Client requests do not expand scope of practice; out-of-scope advice raises liability.

nasm-cpt-readiness-check-nutrition-biz-0.explanation: Risk management combines screening, documentation, informed consent, competence, staying in scope, and referral.
